set.title: Financial literacy: budgets & transactions · Unit Test

questions.question: Jayden's chequing account in Kelowna shows a running balance of $142.60. He taps his debit card to pay $38.75 for a bus pass. What is his new running balance?
questions.explain: A debit-card purchase takes money out, so subtract: $142.60 − $38.75 = $103.85. The classic trap is adding the transaction (giving $181.35) — always ask first whether money went in or out.

questions.question: Nadia puts $600 into a savings account that pays 4% simple interest per year. She leaves it there for 2 years. How much interest does she earn?
questions.explain: Use I = P × r × t with the rate as a decimal: 600 × 0.04 × 2 = $48.00. Two common traps are writing 4% as 0.4 (which gives $480) and answering with the total $648 instead of the interest.

questions.question: Priya's monthly income is $340. Her expenses for the month are: bus pass $52, phone plan $35, snacks $48, movies $65. If she spends nothing else, how much is left for savings?
questions.explain: Add all expenses first (52 + 35 + 48 + 65 = $200), then subtract from income: 340 − 200 = $140. The trap is stopping at the expense total, or missing one line of the list when adding.

questions.question: Two friends open savings accounts. Amir deposits $600 at 2.5% simple interest for 3 years. Bella deposits $900 at 2% simple interest for 2 years. Who earns more interest, and by how much?
questions.explain: Compute each: Amir 600 × 0.025 × 3 = $45; Bella 900 × 0.02 × 2 = $36; so Amir earns $9 more. The trap is assuming the bigger principal always wins — rate and time matter just as much.

questions.question: A phone Marcus wants costs $480 if he saves up and pays cash. The store also offers a plan of $45 per month for 12 months. How much MORE does the payment plan cost in total?
questions.explain: Find the plan's total first (45 × 12 = $540), then subtract the cash price: 540 − 480 = $60 extra. The trap is answering with the plan total $540 instead of the difference.

questions.question: Léa's bank statement for March lists, in order: opening balance $210.00; deposit $75.50; debit purchase $42.30; monthly account fee $4.25; ATM withdrawal $60.00. What is her closing balance?
questions.explain: Work down the list one line at a time: 210.00 + 75.50 − 42.30 − 4.25 − 60.00 = $178.95. The trap is treating the account fee as money coming in, or skipping it because it is small — a fee is always a withdrawal.

questions.question: Sana's monthly income is $240 ($180 babysitting, $60 allowance). Her fixed expenses are phone $25 and bus pass $52. Her variable expenses are snacks $38, gaming $30 and gifts $22. She wants to save $90 each month. How much must she cut from variable spending so the budget balances exactly?
questions.explain: Expenses total $167, so only 240 − 167 = $73 is left, but the savings goal is $90, a shortfall of 90 − 73 = $17. The trap is answering $73 (what she can actually save) instead of the cut needed to reach the goal.

questions.question: Tam has $1,200 from a summer job on Vancouver Island. Account A pays 3% simple interest per year and he would leave the money for 8 months. Account B pays 2% per year and he would leave it for 18 months. Which account gives the greater total, and what is that total?
options: Account A, since its total is $1,224
Account A, since its total is $1,488
Account B, since its total is $1,632
Account B, since its total is $1,236
questions.explain: Change months to years first: A gives 1200 × 0.03 × (8/12) = $24, and B gives 1200 × 0.02 × 1.5 = $36, so B's total is 1200 + 36 = $1,236. The big trap is putting 8 or 18 straight into the formula as years; the second trap is assuming the higher rate always wins.
